You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's subjects and surroundings rendered as drawn forms rather than photographic forms beneath a surface effect?
node.criteria: Pass if the principal subjects and surrounding scene are consistently represented through drawn contours, marks and shading, so the image reads as a drawing rather than a photograph with an added texture. Fail if substantial regions retain photographic surface detail or tonal modeling beneath chalk-like grain or smudging. Recognizable anatomy, fine drawn detail and retained colors do not themselves constitute failure. Return unknown only when the images are unavailable or insufficient to judge.
node.binding: Compare the input and edited images for the requested transformation into a chalk-made drawing, examining the giraffes' bodies and markings as well as the vegetation, ground and background.

node_traces.evidence: The edited scene reads as a chalk drawing: the giraffes have visibly outlined, sketch-like contours and marked shading, while the vegetation, ground, and background are broadly rendered with smudged strokes rather than retaining the source photograph's fine surface detail. The scene remains recognizable, but substantial regions do not appear photographic beneath a mere grain overlay.

response.content: {"text":"The binding is already well targeted, but the trace’s “pass” conflicts with its own evidence: it says substantial regions lack photographic detail beneath a grain overlay, while the criterion requires consistent drawn rendering across subjects and surroundings. Make the decision explicitly assess both the giraffes and the full environment against that criterion, distinguishing chalk-like marks or smudging from mere texture while allowing recognizable anatomy and retained color. Do not infer completion from sketch-like giraffe contours alone; the edited image retains recognizable photographic structure in places, so weigh mixed evidence and use the rubric’s partial outcome when progress is clear but the requested transformation is not complete. Preserve unknown for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not as a substitute for resolving mixed evidence."}
